explanations.answer: Decide who is God and follow
explanations.explanation: Elijah, the LORD's prophet, puts it plain: "If the LORD is God, follow Him. But if Baal is God, follow him." (1 Kings 18:21) Baal is a false god. So he isn't asking for a mood or a maybe. He's asking for a choice, and then for following.

explanations.answer: Keep both gods just to be safe
explanations.explanation: Keeping both is exactly the wavering Elijah is calling out. He asks, "How long will you waver between two opinions?" (1 Kings 18:21) Baal is a false god, and Elijah's "if…but if" gives two options to pick from, not a package deal. Playing it safe sounds smart until you notice you're still standing in the middle.

explanations.answer: Wait and see what happens next
explanations.explanation: Waiting and seeing is just wavering that went and bought a comfy chair. Elijah, the LORD's prophet, says, "If the LORD is God, follow Him. But if Baal is God, follow him." (1 Kings 18:21) Baal is a false god. His words point to following whichever one is God, not sitting on the sidelines.

I get why you'd picture a big roar. But the text says, "But the people did not answer a word." (1 Kings 18:21) No shout, no cheer, no "we choose You!" Just a whole mountain of people holding their tongues.
That's right, friend. After Elijah's challenge, "the people did not answer a word." (1 Kings 18:21) Not a shout, not a whisper. Picture a whole crowd on a mountain and not one of them says a thing.

explanations.answer: Call on the name of its god
explanations.explanation: That's the plan. Elijah says, "Then you may call on the name of your god, and I will call on the name of the LORD." (1 Kings 18:24) Both bulls are on the wood with no fire lit, so each side calls on its god. The one who answers settles it.

explanations.answer: Wait for the people to vote
explanations.explanation: No ballot boxes on this mountain. Elijah says each side will call on the name of its god, and then "The God who answers by fire, He is God." (1 Kings 18:24) The people do answer, "What you say is good," but that's agreeing to the plan, not voting on a winner. The answer itself decides it.

Ahab is king of Israel, and he's the one who summoned everybody to Carmel (1 Kings 18:20). But Elijah never hands him a judge's seat. The test is that each side calls on its god, and "The God who answers by fire, He is God." (1 Kings 18:24) The fire does the deciding.
Fire it is. Elijah says, "The God who answers by fire, He is God." (1 Kings 18:24) Both bulls sit on the wood with nothing lit. So whoever sends the flame has answered.

Rain does show up in this story, but later on, and it isn't the test. Elijah says, "The God who answers by fire, He is God." (1 Kings 18:24) The bulls are on the wood with no fire lit, so fire is what everybody is waiting to see.

Wind isn't what Elijah names here. He says, "The God who answers by fire, He is God." (1 Kings 18:24) Wood on an altar with no flame lit is waiting on one thing. A good breeze won't light my oven either, friend.
Right. After Elijah lays out the plan, "all the people answered, 'What you say is good.'" (1 Kings 18:24) Remember, they'd said nothing a moment before. Now they're on board.

The text says otherwise, friend. When Elijah lays out the plan, "all the people answered, 'What you say is good.'" (1 Kings 18:24) They'd been silent a few verses earlier, so this is a change. Now they agree to the test.

Yes, ma'am, yes, sir. Elijah says to the prophets of Baal, "Since you are so numerous, choose for yourselves one bull and prepare it first." (1 Kings 18:25) They have four hundred and fifty prophets to his one, so they go first. Then he adds, "…do not light the fire."

It's actually true, and the text says so. Elijah tells the prophets of Baal, "Since you are so numerous, choose for yourselves one bull and prepare it first." (1 Kings 18:25) They go first, and the one rule is that they don't light the fire. Elijah's side waits its turn.

Silence. The text says, "But there was no sound, and no one answered as they leaped around the altar they had made." (1 Kings 18:26) They shouted from morning until noon. All that effort, and the only sound was their own.

Not even a spark, friend. The fire was never supposed to be lit by hand, and the text says, "But there was no sound, and no one answered as they leaped around the altar they had made." (1 Kings 18:26) The wood sat there, just as dry and just as unlit as before.

No thunder, no rumble, nothing. The text says, "But there was no sound, and no one answered as they leaped around the altar they had made." (1 Kings 18:26) They shouted from morning until noon. The sky never said a word.

Yes. Elijah says, "Perhaps he is deep in thought, or occupied, or on a journey. Perhaps he is sleeping and must be awakened!" (1 Kings 18:27) He's taunting the prophets of Baal. That's a whole list of excuses, and I've used a few of them on my own snooze button.

It's true, and the text lists them. Elijah says, "Perhaps he is deep in thought, or occupied, or on a journey. Perhaps he is sleeping and must be awakened!" (1 Kings 18:27) Journey and sleeping are both in there. He's taunting the prophets of Baal.

They don't go quiet, friend. The text says, "So they shouted louder and cut themselves with knives and lances, as was their custom, until the blood gushed over them." (1 Kings 18:28) This part is heavy. They kept going.

That's right. The text says, "So they shouted louder and cut themselves with knives and lances, as was their custom, until the blood gushed over them." (1 Kings 18:28) This part is heavy. Instead of going quiet, they kept at it.

Right. The text says, "Midday passed, and they kept on raving until the time of the evening sacrifice." (1 Kings 18:29) They started in the morning, so that's a long day of calling. And the verse ends, "there was no response; no one answered, no one paid attention."

They don't go through the night. The text says they "kept on raving until the time of the evening sacrifice." (1 Kings 18:29) That's a full day already, from morning on. It still ends the same way: "no one answered, no one paid attention."

Ahab, king of Israel, isn't the one who stops it. The text says they "kept on raving until the time of the evening sacrifice." (1 Kings 18:29) The time of day is the marker, not any order from the king. And it ends with "no one answered, no one paid attention."
He sure does. The text says he "repaired the altar of the LORD that had been torn down." (1 Kings 18:30) Elijah doesn't toss it aside for a fresh one. He picks up the broken one and fixes it.

Elijah doesn't walk past it. The text says, "he repaired the altar of the LORD that had been torn down." (1 Kings 18:30) It was a pile, and he made it an altar again. I know a thing or two about being pulled out of a pile, friend.

explanations.answer: He tells Ahab to fix it
explanations.explanation: No delegating here. The text says Elijah himself "repaired the altar of the LORD that had been torn down." (1 Kings 18:30) He tells the people to come near, and then he gets to work. Ahab, Israel's king, isn't given the job.

explanations.answer: One for each tribe of Jacob's sons
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. Elijah took twelve stones, "one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the LORD had come and said, 'Israel shall be your name.'" (1 Kings 18:31) The twelve tribes, all in a pile of stones.

explanations.answer: One for each month of the year
explanations.explanation: Twelve months is a tidy match, I'll give you that. But the text gives a different reason: "one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob." (1 Kings 18:31) The stones stand for the tribes, not the calendar.

explanations.answer: One for each man helping him
explanations.explanation: The text never counts any helpers. It says he took twelve stones, "one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the LORD had come and said, 'Israel shall be your name.'" (1 Kings 18:31) So the number is about the tribes.

Water, friend. Elijah says, "Fill four waterpots and pour the water on the offering and on the wood." (1 Kings 18:34) He's making the fire's job harder on purpose. I've never seen a baker do that, and I've seen plenty.

Oil would help a fire along, but that isn't what Elijah asks for. He says, "Fill four waterpots and pour the water on the offering and on the wood." (1 Kings 18:34) It's water, and not a little. So the altar gets harder to light, not easier.

Sand isn't in this scene. Elijah says, "Fill four waterpots and pour the water on the offering and on the wood." (1 Kings 18:34) It's water poured on the offering and the wood. Sand would at least be dry, and that's the opposite of what he asks for.

Yes. Elijah says, "Fill four waterpots and pour the water on the offering and on the wood." Then, "Do it a second time," and "Do it a third time." (1 Kings 18:34) That's three rounds, and the text says they did it each time.

It's true, and the text counts it out. Elijah says, "Fill four waterpots and pour the water on the offering and on the wood." Then, "Do it a second time," and "Do it a third time." (1 Kings 18:34) They did each round just as he said.

explanations.answer: That He is God in Israel
explanations.explanation: That's the heart of his prayer. Elijah says, "O LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known this day that You are God in Israel and that I am Your servant and have done all these things at Your command." (1 Kings 18:36) He prays for the LORD to be known, and he calls himself the LORD's servant.

The drought is on everyone's mind, but it isn't in this prayer. Elijah asks, "…let it be known this day that You are God in Israel and that I am Your servant and have done all these things at Your command." (1 Kings 18:36) The prayer is about who God is. Rain comes later in the story.

Elijah doesn't mention Ahab, Israel's king, in this prayer. He asks, "…let it be known this day that You are God in Israel and that I am Your servant and have done all these things at Your command." (1 Kings 18:36) It's about the LORD being known and Elijah being His servant.

Yes. Elijah prays, "Answer me, O LORD! Answer me, so that this people will know that You, the LORD, are God, and that You have turned their hearts back again." (1 Kings 18:37) He asks twice for an answer. And he asks for it so the people will know.

It's true, and the prayer says it plainly. Elijah says, "Answer me, O LORD! Answer me, so that this people will know that You, the LORD, are God, and that You have turned their hearts back again." (1 Kings 18:37) The turning back of their hearts is right there in his words.

Not even close, friend. The text says, "Then the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and it licked up the water in the trench." (1 Kings 18:38) Stones, dust and water all went, not only the bull.

That's right. The text says, "Then the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, and the dust, and it licked up the water in the trench." (1 Kings 18:38) It took the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, the dust and the water. Nothing was left out.

explanations.answer: Fall facedown and say the LORD is God
explanations.explanation: That's what they do. "When all the people saw this, they fell facedown and said, 'The LORD, He is God! The LORD, He is God!'" (1 Kings 18:39) A while earlier they had no words at all. Now they say it twice.

explanations.answer: Run down the mountain in fear
explanations.explanation: The text has them going down, not running. It says, "When all the people saw this, they fell facedown and said, 'The LORD, He is God! The LORD, He is God!'" (1 Kings 18:39) The text doesn't say they ran, and it doesn't say they were afraid. They stayed, and they spoke.

explanations.answer: Turn and go back to their homes
explanations.explanation: Nobody is heading for the door here. The text says, "When all the people saw this, they fell facedown and said, 'The LORD, He is God! The LORD, He is God!'" (1 Kings 18:39) They're on the ground, and they're talking. The silence from earlier is over.

That isn't what happens, friend. Elijah orders, "Seize the prophets of Baal! Do not let a single one escape." Then the text says, "So they seized them." (1 Kings 18:40) This part is heavy, and the text says the order was followed.
Right. Elijah orders, "Seize the prophets of Baal! Do not let a single one escape." Then the text says, "So they seized them." (1 Kings 18:40) This part is heavy. The order was followed.

That's it. Elijah says to Ahab, king of Israel, "Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of a heavy rain." (1 Kings 18:41) And this comes after a long drought. Elijah's already talking about the sound of rain.

No army marching in this scene. Elijah tells Ahab, king of Israel, "Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of a heavy rain." (1 Kings 18:41) What he hears is rain. It's good news for a land that's been dry.
No trumpet here. Elijah tells Ahab, king of Israel, "Go up, eat and drink, for there is the sound of a heavy rain." (1 Kings 18:41) He's hearing rain, not a horn.

explanations.answer: Bends down with his face between his knees
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says Elijah "climbed to the summit of Carmel, bent down on the ground, and put his face between his knees." (1 Kings 18:42) Ahab heads off to eat and drink. Elijah goes up and bends low.

explanations.answer: Builds a second altar to the LORD
explanations.explanation: He already built his altar earlier on Carmel. Up at the summit, the text says he "bent down on the ground, and put his face between his knees." (1 Kings 18:42) No stones this time, just Elijah bent low.

explanations.answer: Lights a big fire to signal Ahab
explanations.explanation: No fire this time. The text says Elijah "climbed to the summit of Carmel, bent down on the ground, and put his face between his knees." (1 Kings 18:42) Ahab, king of Israel, is off eating and drinking. Elijah is bent low on the ground.
He does. The servant says, "There is nothing there," and the text says, "Seven times Elijah said, 'Go back.'" (1 Kings 18:43) Nothing there is not the last word. The servant goes again.

It's true, and the text counts it out. After the servant says, "There is nothing there," the text says, "Seven times Elijah said, 'Go back.'" (1 Kings 18:43) Elijah sends him back to look again, and again.
A cloud. On the seventh time the servant reports, "There is a cloud as small as a man's hand rising from the sea." (1 Kings 18:44) That's small. And it's the first thing he's seen all day.

A bird would be easy to spot, but the text says otherwise. The servant reports, "There is a cloud as small as a man's hand rising from the sea." (1 Kings 18:44) It's a cloud, and a small one. Elijah won't be needing binoculars, but it helps.
A sail would at least mean a boat. But the servant reports, "There is a cloud as small as a man's hand rising from the sea." (1 Kings 18:44) Not a sail, a cloud. A small one, rising.

explanations.answer: Get your chariot and go before the rain stops you
explanations.explanation: That's the message. Elijah says, "Go and tell Ahab, 'Prepare your chariot and go down before the rain stops you.'" (1 Kings 18:44) Ahab is the king of Israel. A cloud as small as a hand, and Elijah already has a message about the rain.

explanations.answer: Stay up on the mountain until the storm passes
explanations.explanation: It's the opposite. Elijah says, "Go and tell Ahab, 'Prepare your chariot and go down before the rain stops you.'" (1 Kings 18:44) Ahab is the king of Israel. The message is to go down before the rain stops him.

explanations.answer: Bring the people back for another sacrifice
explanations.explanation: No second sacrifice in this message. Elijah says, "Go and tell Ahab, 'Prepare your chariot and go down before the rain stops you.'" (1 Kings 18:44) Ahab is the king of Israel. It's a message about his chariot and the rain.

Jezreel it is. The text says, "So Ahab rode away and went to Jezreel." (1 Kings 18:45) The sky had gone dark with clouds and wind, and heavy rain was falling. The king of Israel is off in his chariot.
Not Samaria, friend. The text says, "So Ahab rode away and went to Jezreel." (1 Kings 18:45) Heavy rain is falling and the sky is dark. Ahab, Israel's king, has his chariot headed for Jezreel.
Not Bethel. The text says, "So Ahab rode away and went to Jezreel." (1 Kings 18:45) Heavy rain is falling and the sky is dark. Ahab, Israel's king, rides to Jezreel.

Elijah doesn't get a ride. The text says, "the hand of the LORD came upon Elijah, and he tucked his cloak into his belt and ran ahead of Ahab all the way to Jezreel." (1 Kings 18:46) Ahab rode the chariot. Elijah ran in front of him.

That's right. The text says, "the hand of the LORD came upon Elijah, and he tucked his cloak into his belt and ran ahead of Ahab all the way to Jezreel." (1 Kings 18:46) Ahab rode away in his chariot. Elijah ran ahead of him on his own two feet.
